title: The world's best value cities
gist: Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index shows housing costs eating an average 20% of disposable income across the top 100 cities (30% in Vancouver, Auckland and London), while Asia-Pacific cities like Singapore and Canberra uniquely combine high quality of life with lower relative housing costs, and megacities like New York, London and Tokyo keep attracting residents despite scoring poorly on this 'value' mix because of unmatched labour-market scale.

insights.claim: Residents of the top 100 cities in the 2026 Global Cities Index spend an average of 20% of disposable income on housing and utilities, with wide city-level variation that has widened over recent decades.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A 20% average masks acute local affordability crises; investors in residential/rental assets should treat city-level dispersion, not the average, as the signal.
insights.quote: We estimate that residents in the top 100 cities in the 2026 Global Cities Index spend an average of 20% of their disposable income on housing and utilities

insights.claim: Vancouver, Auckland and London sit at the extreme end of housing cost burden, with residents spending roughly 30% of disposable income on housing and utilities, and substantially more in central neighbourhoods.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Flags these markets as structurally rent/price-stressed for residential real estate and wage-competitiveness analysis; central submarkets carry even greater affordability risk.
insights.locator: At the upper end of the spending spectrum

insights.claim: Affordability has become stretched across many city housing markets because excess demand and chronic undersupply are pushing rents and house prices up faster than real incomes.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A structural demand/supply imbalance thesis for urban housing that supports continued rent growth and land-constrained development plays in undersupplied gateway cities.
insights.locator: This is because affordability in many markets

insights.claim: Canberra, Singapore, Taipei and Hong Kong are the standout cities combining lower relative housing costs with higher quality of life, and this cluster is concentrated in the Asia Pacific region.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific regional cluster of cities offering a better cost-of-living-to-livability trade-off, useful for relocation, talent-strategy, or urban real estate allocation decisions.
insights.locator: The best-performing cities when comparing both metrics

insights.claim: Canberra tops the Quality of Life ranking on the back of long life expectancy, low income inequality and high average incomes driven by an abundance of stable, well-paid government jobs, while its planned urban layout frees up land for development more readily than rivals like Sydney and Melbourne.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A planned-city, public-sector-employment model structurally eases housing supply constraints versus peer capitals, a factor to weigh in Australian city-level real estate and labour comparisons.
insights.locator: Canberra, in particular, tops our Quality of Life category

insights.claim: Singapore's state-led housing model—large-scale public housebuilding plus generous ownership grants—keeps prices in check, has significantly boosted homeownership rates, and made expensive rents far less common than in comparable global cities.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A concrete policy mechanism (state-subsidized mass housebuilding) that materially caps housing cost burden; a template other high-cost markets could adopt, and a factor limiting Singapore private-rental upside versus peer megacities.
insights.locator: For Singapore, a high life expectancy

insights.claim: The author suggests western cities such as London may want to emulate the Asian state-led housing supply/subsidy model to address their own affordability crises.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Signals a potential future policy direction (state-led housing supply) for chronically undersupplied western gateway cities like London, relevant to housing-policy and REIT/regulatory risk watchers.
insights.quote: this state-led model is something that peers in the west, such as London, may wish to emulate
insights.locator: Other Asian cities also perform relatively well

themes.theme: Smaller European 'value' cities losing their edge

insights.claim: Vienna's public housing-focused model makes it more affordable than similarly sized European peer cities while still ranking as a desirable place to live.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Reinforces that public-housing-heavy policy regimes (not just Asia's) can decouple livability from housing cost inflation, a comparator for European urban policy and real estate risk.
insights.locator: Vienna is another city with a similar public housing-focused model

insights.claim: Valletta (Malta) and Ljubljana (Slovenia) currently offer good value among smaller European capitals, but both are becoming markedly more expensive as strong demand from fast-growing local economies erodes their affordability, with Valletta additionally squeezed by limited space and a sharp rise in short-term holiday rentals tied to its tourism boom.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Flags Valletta and Ljubljana as 'value' cities with a closing window—an early-cycle signal for rising housing costs and tourism-driven short-term-rental displacement pressure in these markets.
insights.quote: the time of these cities as ‘affordable’ locations may be coming to an end, even if the quality of life offered is high

themes.theme: The megacity paradox: poor 'value' but enduring pull

insights.claim: New York, London and Tokyo score poorly on the combined affordability-quality of life measure because housing costs are so high relative to incomes, yet they retain unmatched global appeal.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Confirms megacity housing markets can stay structurally expensive without denting demand, supporting a long-term bull case for prime real estate and rents in these gateway cities despite weak 'value' scores.
insights.locator: One notable feature of this type of analysis

insights.claim: Residents choose megacities despite high costs because the scale of labour market opportunities and access to world-leading cultural and recreational amenities are unrivalled elsewhere, making higher living costs a rational trade-off rather than a market failure.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A mental model for why megacity housing demand is inelastic to cost: value migrants trade housing cost against labour-market depth and amenity access, a useful lens for forecasting migration and rent resilience.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics does not expect the fundamentals behind megacity appeal to change soon, expecting New York, London and Tokyo-type 'superstar cities' to keep attracting and retaining residents, particularly younger workers who need deep labour markets to advance their careers.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A multi-year demand-durability call for megacity housing and labour markets, supporting continued investment conviction in prime residential and office assets in these gateway cities.
insights.quote: We don’t expect these fundamentals to change anytime soon, and so these superstar cities will continue to offer enough value to attract and retain residents.
insights.locator: We don’t expect these fundamentals to change

insights.claim: Smaller high quality-of-life cities such as Canberra and Valletta cannot and do not aim to compete with London, New York, Paris, Tokyo and Los Angeles on the scale of economic and cultural opportunity that anchors megacity demand.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Sets a ceiling on how much 'value' cities can structurally divert megacity-bound talent and capital, limiting the competitive threat smaller high-QoL cities pose to prime gateway city real estate.
insights.locator: Smaller cities, no matter how high the quality of life

insights.claim: The 2026 Global Cities Index scores cities across five categories—Economics, Human Capital, Quality of Life, Environment and Governance—and its Quality of Life sub-score combines access to recreation/culture, life expectancy, crime rates, income equality, income per person and housing expenditure as a share of disposable income (with housing expenditure stripped out in this report to avoid double counting against the affordability metric).
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Clarifies the underlying methodology so investors and analysts can replicate or stress-test the city rankings rather than taking 'best value' claims at face value.
